title: Hanukkah: the lights
hookLine: a small revolt, a rededicated Temple, and eight nights of lights in the window
last: FINISH AND BEGIN THE SAME DAY.

cards: A winter evening, a street of lit windows. In some, a row of small flames: two, three, maybe eight, with one standing a little higher or off to the side.
Candles in a silver holder, little cups of olive oil, a child's clay creation. They're not hidden in the dining room. They're in the window, facing the street, on purpose.
Whoever lit them wants you, a stranger driving by, to see them. That's part of the point.

teach.b: Hanukkah means dedication. The story is told in the books of the Maccabees.
The land of Israel was ruled by a Greek-speaking kingdom, and its king, Antiochus the Fourth, outlawed Jewish practice: Shabbat, circumcision, Torah study.
The Temple in Jerusalem was turned over to the worship of other gods. A priestly family, led by an old man named Mattathias and then his son Judah, called the Maccabee, led a small revolt.
Against the odds, they won back Jerusalem, cleaned the Temple, and rededicated it, on the twenty-fifth of the month of Kislev.
Those books aren't part of the Hebrew Bible, and the festival isn't in the Torah: Hanukkah was set by the rabbis. Then the Talmud adds the oil.

teach.h: A SMALL REVOLT, A CLEANED TEMPLE.
teach.b: When the Temple was retaken, there was only one small jar of pure oil left, enough to light the Temple menorah for one day. It burned for eight.

teach.h: ONE JAR OF OIL, EIGHT NIGHTS.
LIGHTS IN THE WINDOW, TO BE SEEN.
teach.b: And the Talmud gives the lights a job: to publicize the miracle. That's why they go in a doorway or a window facing the street, lit while people are still out walking.
The lamp is often called a hanukkiah: eight lights, plus a helper light, the shamash, used to light the others.
Hanukkah isn't one of the major holidays in Jewish law; work goes on as normal. But it's built to be seen. For a people once told not to be seen practicing, the whole mitzvah is to be seen.

how: For eight nights from the 25th of Kislev, Jewish families light a hanukkiah, adding one light each night with the shamash, say blessings, and place it in a window or doorway where passersby can see it.

practice: Picture a single flame in a dark window. Think about something you believe in, or love, that you keep hidden because it might look strange, and just notice it; you don't have to announce anything.
